title: Production Operations & SRE for Go — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Running Go in production requires understanding not just the language but the operational characteristics of the Go runtime: goroutine scheduling, GC pauses, memory allocator behaviour. SRE-focused interviews test whether you can define meaningful SLIs/SLOs, implement graceful shutdown correctly, and diagnose goroutine and memory leaks before they become incidents. These questions separate engineers who have shipped to production from those who haven't.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Production readiness for a Go service has five concerns: (1) Reliability contracts — SLI (what to measure), SLO (target), error budget. (2) Graceful lifecycle — handle SIGTERM, drain in-flight requests, close connections. (3) Goroutine hygiene — every goroutine must have an exit path; use context cancellation + WaitGroup. (4) Memory health — heap profile before and after load, watch for retained references (global maps, caches without eviction). (5) Capacity — benchmark under realistic load, set resource requests/limits from p95 data, configure HPA thresholds.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. SLI/SLO/SLA: SLI = ratio of good requests / total requests; SLO = 99.9% success over 30 days; SLA = contractual commitment with penalties. Error budget = 1 - SLO. 2. Graceful shutdown: signal.NotifyContext, http.Server.Shutdown(ctx), sync.WaitGroup for active requests, close DB pool. 3. Goroutine leak detection: runtime.NumGoroutine in /debug/pprof/goroutine, goleak in tests (uber-go/goleak). 4. Memory leaks: heap pprof, watch for growing alloc_space, common causes: time.Ticker not stopped, unclosed http.Response.Body, growing slice/map. 5. Performance profiling: go tool pprof CPU profile, identify hot functions, benchmark before and after, GOGC tuning for GC pressure. 6. Capacity planning: load test with k6 or vegeta, observe p50/p95/p99 latency and memory under N×current load. 7. Incident response: define runbook, use structured logs for diagnosis, rollback strategy (previous image tag in Kubernetes).

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'How do you implement graceful shutdown in a Go HTTP server?' → signal.NotifyContext for SIGTERM, http.Server.Shutdown with deadline, WaitGroup for background workers. • 'How do you detect a goroutine leak?' → runtime.NumGoroutine in a Prometheus gauge, pprof goroutine profile, goleak in tests. • 'What is an error budget and how do you use it in Go teams?' → 1 - SLO target; if budget is exhausted, freeze new features and focus on reliability. • 'Walk me through diagnosing a memory leak in a Go service.' → heap pprof with -base comparison, look for inuse_space growth, check for unclosed resources, time.Ticker, global maps.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "For graceful shutdown I use signal.NotifyContext to convert SIGTERM into context cancellation. The HTTP server gets http.Server.Shutdown called with a 30-second deadline, and I track all background goroutines with a sync.WaitGroup. The process exits only after all in-flight requests complete and the WaitGroup reaches zero. For goroutine leak detection I expose runtime.NumGoroutine as a Prometheus gauge—a steadily growing value during a load test is a red flag. In tests I use goleak.VerifyNone as a deferred call in TestMain. When I suspect a memory leak I take two heap profiles 60 seconds apart with go tool pprof -alloc_space and compare them; the top inuse_space entries tell me what's accumulating. The most common culprits I've seen are time.Ticker not stopped in background workers and HTTP response bodies not closed."
